query: For high-entropy-alloy materials intended for self-lubricating moving components, what single intervention could reduce both coefficient of friction and wear rate across a wide service-temperature range? Formulate one hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains its mechanism, predicts the improvement relative to the untreated alloy, defines the conditions under which it should remain effective, cites prior evidence supporting it, and proposes an experiment whose outcome could falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Thermal annealing of high-entropy alloys in air promotes the in situ formation of a dense, self-lubricating oxide layer that reduces both the coefficient of friction and wear rate over a wide service-temperature range.
generation.material_initial_state: Untreated HEA with a standard crystalline/amorphous microstructure lacking a protective surface oxide.
generation.intervention: Performing a high-temperature annealing treatment (e.g., at 800°C for 1 hour) in air.
generation.conditions: Oxidative environments and service temperatures ranging from room temperature up to around 800°C, where annealing-induced oxide formation is stable.
generation.structural_mediator: A dense composite oxide layer (for example, a ZrTiO4-type layer) that forms on the alloy surface during annealing.
generation.mechanism: The annealing induces surface oxidation which forms a protective, self-lubricating oxide film. This film minimizes direct metal-to-metal contact during motion, thereby reducing friction and wear simultaneously.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the untreated alloy, the annealed HEA will exhibit a lower coefficient of friction and reduced wear rate across the specified temperature range.
generation.baseline: Untreated HEA surfaces exhibit higher friction and wear due to direct contact and lack a self-forming lubricious oxide layer.
generation.boundary: The intervention is expected to be effective only if the annealing conditions allow for the uniform and complete formation of the oxide layer; rapid thermal fluctuations or nonoxidative environments may mitigate the benefits.
generation.uncertainty: The exact magnitude of friction and wear reduction is not precisely predicted and may vary with alloy composition, annealing duration, and environmental conditions.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of HEA samples. Subject one set to annealing at 800°C for 1 hour in air and leave the other set untreated. Expose both sets to a series of sliding/contact tests over a temperature range from ambient to 800°C. Characterize the surface of annealed samples for oxide layer formation using spectroscopic and microscopic techniques.
measurements: Coefficient of friction across the temperature range
Wear rate (volume loss per unit load and distance)
Surface oxide composition and uniformity (using XPS/SEM)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the annealed samples do not exhibit a statistically significant decrease in both the coefficient of friction and wear rate, or if the expected dense oxide layer is not confirmed, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: AbstractAlCrTiZrMo high-entropy alloy (HEA) films with strong amorphization were obtained by co-filter cathode vacuum arc deposition, and the effect of thermal shock on the films was investigated in order to explore the protection mechanism of HEA films against mechanical components in extreme service environments. The results show that after annealing at 800 °C for 1 h, the formation of a dense ZrTiO4 composite oxide layer on the surface actively prevents the oxidation from continuing, so that the AlCrTiZrMo HEA film exhibits excellent oxidation resistance at 800 °C in air. In the friction-corrosion coupling environment, the AlCrTiZrMo HEA film annealed at 800 °C for 1 h shows the best tribocorrosion resistance due to the stable dense microstructure and excellent mechanical properties, and its ΔOCP, COF and wear rate possess the smallest values of 0.055, 0.04 and 1.34 × 10−6 mm−3·N−1·m−1.Keywords: AlCrTiZrMo high-entropy alloy film, thermal shock, oxidation, tribocorrosion
